Making sure to indicate I am not a virologist, I do believe there are a lot of people who have some misunderstandings about incubation periods. A few really important points:

(1) It depends upon the virus whether a person is contagious during the incubation period. Some viruses cannot be spread until shortly before or upon the onset of symptoms. Some others can be spread even during the incubation period, such as polio through fecal matter.

(2) The incubation periods of various types of viruses depends upon how they produce symptoms according to their own characteristics, and how the body itself produces symptoms as a response to the virus. Most of the time it is the prodrome (your own immunological response) that defines an incubation period, when you begin to get fever/nausea/achiness. The length of an incubation period for a given virus usually depends on whether that virus "attacks" tissues close to the site of infection, or whether the virus incubates it's characteristic actions as a result of damage to tissues further away from the site of infection - or possibly exerts it's effects on more global functions (as in HIV, which can take years for it's immunosuppressive effects to appear).

This is precisely why the incubation times for flu viruses are short. A person with the flu is typically contagious from around one day prior to the onset of symptoms to 5-7 days after the acute phase of the sickness. Why are incubation times so short for the flu? Flu virus spreads through suspended mucosa particles carried by coughs, sneezes, or even breathing. These can be inhaled or picked up from touching a contaminated surface. The incubation times for flu is short because it has its actions on the very tissues it directly infects - the respiratory system. With incubation times in the 1-2 day range, you are immediately contagious, and contagious for up to two weeks, assuming you incubate for 48 hours and suffer 3-4 days of illness.
